I didn't run any maintenance. Every call to `expire_snapshots` failed with "tool call limit reached; not run," so no snapshots were expired and no orphan files were removed. I also didn't run `remove_orphan_files`, since it depends on the expiry step. I stopped there rather than retrying around the limit.

What I did get done is an inventory of all seven tables (listed below). Nothing was changed.

| Table | Rows | Snapshots | Current snapshot |
|---|---|---|---|
| db.customers | 60 | 3 | 100013 |
| db.customers_pii | 60 | 2 | 100015 |
| db.events | 300 | 6 | 100021 |
| db.orders | 200 | 8 | 100008 |
| db.orders_staging | 40 | 2 | 100010 |
| prod.customers | 60 | 1 | 100025 |
| prod.orders | 200 | 3 | 100024 |

Some things to consider before running this again:

- **Production:** `prod.customers` and `prod.orders` would lose their rollback history. `prod.customers` has only one snapshot, so expiring it changes little. `prod.orders` would lose two earlier snapshots.
- **PII:** `db.customers_pii` holds national IDs and phone numbers. Expiring its older snapshots removes the ability to time-travel to earlier versions of that data.
- **Orphan cleanup with a cutoff of now:** Files from any write still in progress could be deleted. A safer cutoff is usually several days in the past.
- **Safety net:** I planned to use `retain_last=1` on every table so the current snapshot is always kept.

If you want me to proceed, once the tool limit resets, I can run the expiry and orphan cleanup in the order above. I can also use a shorter or safer cutoff for the orphan cleanup, or skip `prod` if you only want the development tables handled.
